Subject: Clarify Redwood default retention (requests vs completions)

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the call earlier. Procurement needs a crisp summary for our security/controls review: what does Redwood keep by default for hosted customers using the API? Specifically:

- Are raw requests (user inputs/prompts) retained? For how long?
- Are model completions (responses) retained, and are streaming fragments treated differently?
- Do function call traces / tool call arguments end up in logs by default?
- What about KV cache, embeddings, or intermediate artifacts (tokenized inputs, attention traces)?
- Where is the data stored (region/residency) and how can we request erasure + get proof?

We need this as a short Q&A we can attach to the procurement packet (one page, bullets + next steps). Can you confirm what you can share and whether you have a downloadable summary / SLA we can include?

Appreciate it — Nathan

Hi Nathan,

Thanks — I've pulled together a concise summary below and attached a one‑page retention brief and our standard SSO/SLA docs for procurement. Copying Karthik and Marissa to add any technical/implementation details.

Quick Q&A (hosted API defaults):
- Requests (raw user input/prompts): retained by default for 30 days. After 30 days requests are removed from the live request store. Aggregates/metrics derived from requests may be stored longer in anonymized form.
- Completions (final responses): retained by default for 30 days. Streaming fragments are buffered during the session and persist transiently; fragments are joined into the session record at completion and follow the same 30‑day horizon.
- Function/tool call arguments & traces: tool call payloads are captured as part of the request/response record by default and follow the same 30‑day retention.
- KV cache: ephemeral by default — per-session KV cache is not persisted to long‑term storage unless explicitly configured by the customer.
- Embeddings and indexes: not created or stored by default. If a customer opts into embeddings/indexing (via the Console or API flag) those artifacts are retained until customer deletion/retention policy takes effect.
- Tokenization/provenance: tokenized representations used for runtime are not exported as separate persistent artifacts by default.
- Residency: default data storage region follows the account region configured at signup (us/eu/apac). We can pin or migrate residency for enterprise contracts.
- Erasure: customers can request deletion via the Console or the /v1/accounts/erase API. Standard proof-of-deletion is a signed deletion token and an exportable audit record (Doc ID) showing the timeline and SHA256 checksum of removed objects; Support can provide the Doc ID and certificate.

Next steps I recommend: (1) Attach the two files I sent (one‑pager + SLA) to your packet; (2) If you need a residency commitment addendum, Marissa can route to Legal; (3) If you want stricter default retention we can enable a 0‑retain option at account creation for enterprise customers (requires an addendum).

I'll let Karthik add any nuance about streaming vs session finalization.

Thanks,
Kimberly

Nathan — quick technical clarifications to the points Kimberly shared. Quoting the relevant lines: 

> "Streaming fragments are buffered during the session and persist transiently; fragments are joined into the session record at completion and follow the same 30‑day horizon."

- Implementation detail: streaming fragments are held in an in‑memory buffer for low-latency delivery. For fault tolerance we replicate the minimal append buffer to a short‑lived durable store (replica TTL = 2 hours) so sessions can recover from node failure — these short-lived replicas are rotated and purged automatically. Only after the session finalizes do fragments get materialized into the session record that lives in the request/response store (30d). If a customer requests deletion mid-session, we fast‑path purge the materialized session record and invalidate the in‑memory session; ephemeral replicas (if any) are also removed as part of the erase flow.

> "Function/tool call arguments are captured as part of the request/response record by default and follow the same 30‑day retention."

- We do capture tool call payloads in the session record by default. For customers concerned about PII we recommend either: (a) client‑side redaction before invoking tools, or (b) enable 'no-store' at account/route level via the Console (enterprise option). We do not perform automatic PII redaction.

About proof-of-deletion: our standard deliverable includes the list of internal record IDs and the storage keys that were removed plus a signed audit row (time, actor, reason). For hosted customers in enterprise contracts we can provide an S3 key list and a signed deletion manifest; for self‑serve customers we provide the deletion token and high‑level audit record.

I can summarize the above into a 2‑paragraph technical note for procurement. If BrightBank wants object-level manifests and SLA language we will need to add that to the contract (we have a template we can share).
